Before you confirm, the question names the backup: Motif does not back up your project, so back it up in FieldWorks first (How to Back Up a Project in FieldWorks opens FieldWorks' own help). Confirm Apply only when you want those changes written to FieldWorks.
entries.helpPage:
# Apply to FieldWorks

In **Proposals**, open the Proposal you want to apply and read its proposed changes, Rationale and evidence. Complete **Before you apply**, then choose **Apply…**. Motif activates that Proposal, reads its current review and checks whether Apply is available. Before you confirm, the question names the backup: Motif does not back up your project, so back it up in FieldWorks first (**How to Back Up a Project in FieldWorks** opens FieldWorks' own help). Confirm **Apply** only when you want those changes written to FieldWorks.

Every change must still fit. The project's evidence and the Proposal's Trial must be current and complete enough for the engine's readiness rules. A held FieldWorks project, lost approved analysis, dropped grammar or an unresolved previous Apply can prevent writing. **Apply…** stays off until the Proposal has a current Trial, a Difference from that try and a Dry Run recorded for the Proposal. The checklist shows the actions to take on the Proposal document. Use **Refresh** if FieldWorks changed. Choose **Try Again** when the Trial is outdated and **Run Dry Run** when the checklist asks for it. Follow any additional guidance beside Apply. The window does not offer a force action.

A successful Apply shows the real Receipt. It makes the evidence of other open Proposals outdated, so measure them again before deciding. After an unconfirmed write, FieldWorks may already have these changes. Check the project and choose **Refresh** before trying Apply again. The window provides no post-Apply Undo; staged-change Undo applies only before changes have been applied.

entries.title: Working with Claude
entries.description: Claude is not in Motif's window. You work with Claude in Claude Desktop, through the MCP, and there is no Ask Claude action, Claude button or panel in Motif.
entries.helpPage:
# Working with Claude

Claude is not in Motif's window. You work with Claude in Claude Desktop, through the MCP, and there is no Ask Claude action, Claude button or panel in Motif.

In Claude Desktop, name a Proposal, a Comment, a Grammar Guide section, a word, a word group or a Passage, with an optional note. Claude records a Request about that exact item. A Request waits for Claude to draft a Proposal; it does not apply a change or approve an analysis.

Read and review a returned Proposal in **Proposals** before deciding whether to Apply it. To set up Claude Desktop, see [Connect an assistant](guide:ai-assistants).

entries.title: Parse all words
entries.description: Parse all words asks PanGloss to parse the words you chose and keeps the result with the version of the project and the words it measured.
entries.helpPage:
# Parse all words

**Parse all words** asks PanGloss to parse the words you chose and keeps the result with the version of the project and the words it measured.

While it runs, the progress panel stays visible at the top of the window. It shows how many words are done, the word currently being parsed, elapsed time and an estimate of the time left. It also shows the slowest word so far, with its parser work, and lists words that stopped at the work limit or the time safety net, each with its parser work. If no word finishes for a long time, the panel explains that the parser may have stalled and offers **Cancel** and **Report a problem**.

The result tells you which words parsed, which approved analyses PanGloss built again, and the time on this computer. Parser work gives a more stable measure for comparing grammar changes. A search that was interrupted or stopped at a limit is saved as not finished; it should not be read as a completed “no parse.” The **Progress** and **Texts** pages read the saved result. Opening either page does not run PanGloss.

After saving in FieldWorks, choose **Refresh** (the ⟳ beside the project name in the top bar) to read the saved project, then **Parse all words** in the project card to parse your [Default Selection](term:default-selection) again. A parse is evidence about one run, not a verdict that the grammar is good or bad.

Motif allows only one Parse all words run for a project at a time, even across windows and processes. If another window is already parsing that project, a second request is refused; use the running window to follow progress or cancel the run.

entries.title: Baseline
entries.description: A Baseline is Motif’s saved reference copy of a FieldWorks project. Motif uses it to reproduce parser behavior and to compare later results with the project state it measured. It reads the .fwdata file on disk, so the Baseline reflects FieldWorks’ last save, not edits still open and unsaved there.
entries.helpPage:
# Baseline

A [Baseline](term:baseline) is Motif’s saved reference copy of a FieldWorks project. Motif uses it to reproduce parser behavior and to compare later results with the project state it measured. It reads the `.fwdata` file on disk, so the Baseline reflects FieldWorks’ last save, not edits still open and unsaved there.

The Baseline is not a backup of linked media, and it is not a live view of FieldWorks. It stays in place until you capture another one. When a project has no Baseline, Motif captures one the first time you open it, then asks what to measure. Later, **Refresh** captures a new Baseline; **Parse all words** measures your chosen words against it. Opening a project with a Baseline reads it and the results already stored.

If the project has changed since the Baseline, Motif can mark its stored numbers as stale. A stale parse and a change that says **No longer fits** are related to different things: one is old measurement evidence; the other is a particular pending choice that no longer matches the project. See [Drift](term:drift).

entries.title: Building a grammar: a suggested order
entries.description: This page describes the order in which linguists usually build a morphological grammar for FieldWorks, and the reason for each step. It is advice, not a rule. Motif does not check, enforce or remember where you are in it, and nothing in the window is greyed out or reordered by it. Motif has no setting for the type of language, and FieldWorks has none either. Work in whatever order your language and your data suggest, and go back to any part when a test shows a gap.
entries.helpPage:
# Building a grammar: a suggested order

This page describes the order in which linguists usually build a morphological grammar for FieldWorks, and the reason for each step. It is advice, not a rule. Motif does not check, enforce or remember where you are in it, and nothing in the window is greyed out or reordered by it. Motif has no setting for the type of language, and FieldWorks has none either. Work in whatever order your language and your data suggest, and go back to any part when a test shows a gap.

The method follows H. Andrew Black, *A Conceptual Introduction to Morphological Parsing for FieldWorks Language Explorer* (SIL, 3 July 2025), which ships in the FieldWorks 9 Help. Black organises his guide by mechanism, not as a numbered procedure. The order below is our reading of his tips and worked examples, so where it says "Black §2.1.1" it names the section that supports one step, not a sequence he sets out himself. Lessons from our own grammar builds are labelled **In our experience**; they are not from Black or from any textbook.

Black states the goal this way: "The idea is to use the morphotactic mechanisms to correctly describe the facts of the language and thereby not only provide correct parses, but also rule out false parses" (§2, opening). So the aim is a grammar that parses what is a word and does not parse what is not. Neither Black nor Motif sets a percentage to reach.

You make grammar and lexicon changes in FieldWorks. Motif shows what the parser did with them: save in FieldWorks, choose **Refresh**, then [Parse all words](term:parse-all-words) to measure again.

## Texts and words to test on

**What to do.** Choose some Texts you have interlinearized, and add any extra words you care about. This is your [Default Selection](term:default-selection), the words Motif measures every time. Mark spellings you know are not words as Incorrect spelling.

**Why.** Texts give you real words to test every later step against, and measuring the same words each time lets you compare one run with the next. Fieldwork textbooks place connected texts alongside the rest of the work: Claire Bowern, *Linguistic Fieldwork* (2nd ed., 2015), has a chapter titled "Discourse, Pragmatics, and Narrative Data" (chapter 9).

Our own suggestion, which has no source: Motif measures only the Default Selection, so you can leave one Text out of it and add it later to see how the grammar does on words you did not tune it to.

**In Motif.** Setup asks you to choose texts or add words in **What Should Motif Measure Every Time?**; choose **Configure…** from the project menu to change it later (see [Choosing what to measure](guide:first-run-setup)). In **Texts** or **Words**, choose **Set analysis** on a word and mark its spelling Incorrect; the change stays pending until you review and apply it in **Proposals** (see [Texts](guide:texts) and [Keyboard shortcuts](guide:keyboard-shortcuts)).

## Sounds

**What to do.** Define the phonemes and natural classes before anything refers to them. If you will use phonological rules, give the phonemes features too; Black's worked example creates the features, makes sure every phoneme is defined, assigns the features, then writes the rules.

**Why.** Black §3.1.3 says environments for allomorphs are defined "once the set of phonemes and natural classes are defined", and §3.1.1 says you need a list of all the phonemes to use environments or natural classes. For the rule-based parser, §6.2.1 says every phoneme used in the orthography must be defined, and a word with even one undefined phoneme is "guaranteed to not give an analysis"; §6.2.2 says features must give each phoneme a distinct set of values; §6.2.3 and §6.2.4 say to be as specific as practical. Black's worked example in §6.1.2.1.4.1 (Figure 51) runs: create the features, make sure every phoneme is defined, assign the features, then write ordered rules. The fieldwork textbooks also take sounds first: Bowern's chapter 5 is titled "Fieldwork on Phonetics and Phonology", before chapters 6 and 7 on morphology and syntax.

**In Motif.** A word PanGloss cannot read shows **PanGloss can’t read it** with its recorded reason. If the reason names the project’s phonemes, inspect the phoneme inventory before parsing again (see [Texts](guide:texts)). **Why This Analysis?** traces the selected word (see [Why This Analysis?](guide:why-this-analysis)).

## Words and their parts

**What to do.** Work out the morphemes by comparing forms, for example, forms that share a part with the same meaning. Enter roots, stems and affixes as lexical entries, each with the right morpheme type. When you know whether an affix is inflectional or derivational, say so.

**Why.** Black §1.2 lists what a parser must know: the forms and glosses of prefixes, infixes, roots and suffixes, which affixes go with which roots, their relative order, and when a shape is legitimate. For a word made of one morpheme, §2 says to add a lexical entry and set the morpheme type of its allomorph to a root or stem type; §4.2 lists the morpheme types the parser keys on. On classification, §2.1.1 says an unclassified affix "is relatively unconstrained as to where it can appear", so the parser may return incorrect parses, and "the best solution, of course, is to classify the affix as being either inflectional or derivational". §2.1.5 gives criteria for deciding (Bickford's table) and adds that they "are not hard and fast rules". Label an affix unclassified when you do not know yet, and change it when you do.

**In Motif.** Parse your Selection and open **Progress**. [Text Coverage](term:text-coverage) says how many of your chosen words parse. Read it as one measure among several: it is not a score for the grammar (see [Reading project health](guide:reading-the-overview)).

## Where affixes go

**What to do.** Give each category its templates and slots, so affixes appear only in the positions they can occupy.

**Why.** Black §2.1.2.1 to §2.1.2.5 cover templates, optional slots, multiple templates, discontinuous morphemes and the interaction with categories. Black's Morphotactics section (§2) opens by saying morphotactics controls the order of morphemes and which can co-occur.

**In Motif.** After a change in FieldWorks, parse again and open **Why This Analysis?** on a word that should contain the affix. It shows what the parser built and where it stopped.

## Allomorphs

**What to do.** When one morpheme has several shapes, decide what chooses between them. If a sound environment does, use a phonological environment. If it is a lexical property of the stem, use an inflection class. If it tracks something the word agrees with, use a feature.

**Why.** Black §3.1.3 and §3.1.4 cover environments and allomorph ordering; §2.1.2.6 inflection classes; §2.1.2.7 agreement and other inflection features; and §2.1.2.8, Table 9, offers guidelines for choosing between a class and a feature. Order here is ours: Black explains environments in his morphophonemics section and classes and features in the morphotactics section.

**In our experience.** Give each stem its class as you add it. In a Tamil build, a restriction that limited a past-tense suffix to one inflection class made nine types that had parsed stop parsing, because two verb stems had no class yet. Eight parsed again once those two stems were given the class (Tamil checkpoint report).

**In Motif.** The **Lost** list in **Texts** marks a word FieldWorks holds an Approved analysis for that the grammar no longer builds (see [Texts](guide:texts)).

## Agreement

**What to do.** Put the features on the words that are agreed with, and then on the affixes that agree with them. The order is ours; Black §2.1.2.7 shows the mechanism, not a sequence.

**Why.** Black §2.1.2.7 uses Spanish gender to show how inflection features rule out incorrect parses, and Table 8 lists situations where features can do the same.

**In our experience.** In a Swahili build, adjective concord was entered with noun-class features required on the affixes (proposal 0133) before nouns carried the feature (proposal 0134). The build log records that a mismatched noun and adjective could not be shown to fail until the nouns had it (Swahili build report). Later, of the 523 tokens in an annotated sample that a reference marked as real words but the grammar did not parse, 174 needed concord series for function words, the second-largest group after missing lexemes (206). The reference was drafted with AI help and has not been reviewed by a native speaker (Swahili gap report).

## Stem alternations and exceptions

**What to do.** For stems or affixes whose shape changes in ways sound environments do not explain, condition the allomorphs on morphosyntactic features. For single combinations that are simply wrong, mark the exception.

**Why.** Black §3.7 covers non-phonologically conditioned allomorphy, with stem allomorphs and affix allomorphs conditioned by features; §3.8 covers irregularly inflected forms; §2.1.6 covers exception "features", for stems and affixes that combine incorrectly "due to historical or some other seemingly arbitrary reasons".

## Derivation, compounds and clitics

**What to do.** Add derivational affixes, compound rules and clitics once the inflection beneath them is working.

**Why.** Black covers derivational affixes in §2.1.3, stem compounding in §2.2 and clitics in §2.3. The ordering is ours; Black does not say to do these after inflection.

## Ordered phonological rules

**What to do.** Write phonological rules once you have stems and affixes to test them on.

**Why.** Black §6.1.2 notes that these rules are ordered, so that the output of one is the input to the next, and §6.2 lists the checks that make the rule-based parser work. The sequence "once there are stems and affixes to test them on" is ours.

**In Motif.** **Why This Analysis?** lists the rules on the best path of a trace, and says that **Tried** does not mean **Applied** (see [Why This Analysis?](guide:why-this-analysis)).

## Ad hoc rules, last

**What to do.** Use an ad hoc rule only when a wrong parse persists after you have used the other mechanisms.

**Why.** Black §2.4 says to use them "when one has used all the mechanisms provided by the parser to the best of one's ability and such incorrect parses continue to surface"; §3.10 says the same for allomorph-oriented rules.

## Keep null morphemes few

Black §4.1.1 says one "wants to avoid having null allomorphs if for no other reason than that they can make the parser run rather slowly". If a null allomorph is the best analysis, keep it. The **Timing** page shows which words are slow.

## How this varies by type of language

Motif has no typology setting, and FieldWorks has none either. A language's type shows in its grammar, in what you end up needing: templates and slots for rich affixation, affix processes for reduplication or infixation, compound rules, inflection classes and features for agreement systems, and phonological rules where sounds change at morpheme boundaries. A language with little inflection may never need most of these steps; a language with heavy agreement will spend most of its time in the Agreement section. Black's guide has sections for reduplication (§3.2), infixation (§3.3), epenthesis (§3.4), metathesis (§3.5) and incorporation (§2.2.3).

## Optional checks

You may also list a whole closed class, such as all the demonstratives or all the pronouns, and check that each parses. You may also lay out a paradigm table for one stem and look for empty cells. Motif does not measure either one; the checks are yours to run with **Why This Analysis?**.

## Going back

The order loops. Testing shows gaps in earlier work, and Black says as much about affix classification: "as you study the language more, you should eventually figure out whether such affixes are inflectional or derivational" (§2.1). Return to any part when a Parse all words shows a gap. The same holds for false parses: when a word you know is not a word parses, go back to the part that lets it through.

## Further reading

- H. Andrew Black, *A Conceptual Introduction to Morphological Parsing for FieldWorks Language Explorer* (SIL, 2025), in the FieldWorks 9 Help.
- Claire Bowern, *Linguistic Fieldwork: A Practical Guide* (2nd ed., 2015), chapters 5 to 9 and Appendix B, "Suggested Fieldwork Programme for an Undescribed Language".
- Eugene A. Nida, *Morphology: The Descriptive Analysis of Words* (1949).
- The Rapid Word Collection method (rapidwords.net), for gathering vocabulary by semantic domain.

entries.title: Cancelling a run
entries.description: During Parse all words, choose Cancel in the progress panel at the top of the window. The panel stays visible while you move between pages. If no word has finished for a long time, it shows a stalled-search notice; cancel there if you do not want to keep waiting. A second Parse all words request for the same project is refused while the first run is active. Use the window that owns the run to see its progress or cancel it.
entries.helpPage:
# Cancelling a run

During **Parse all words**, choose **Cancel** in the progress panel at the top of the window. The panel stays visible while you move between pages. If no word has finished for a long time, it shows a stalled-search notice; cancel there if you do not want to keep waiting. A second Parse all words request for the same project is refused while the first run is active. Use the window that owns the run to see its progress or cancel it.

Cancel keeps the results from the previous completed parse. The unfinished parse is not saved, and Motif does not change the FieldWorks project. For other long actions, use the **Cancel** control beside the running action: on **Why This Analysis?**, **AI Handoff**, or beside **Re-run chosen words** in **Timing**. The global progress panel also has **Cancel** while **Parse all words** runs.

![Parse all words progress and its Cancel control](shot:first-run-setup-parse/cancelling)

entries.title: Changing an analysis
entries.description: In Texts or Words, find the word, then choose the analysis and the opinion you want for it: approve or disapprove it, or make it Unknown. Opinions change one analysis at a time, in the text. To keep one reading at several places of the same word, use the word panel described in Passage. The available action may vary with the word’s current state and the reading you select.
entries.helpPage:
# Changing an analysis

In **Texts** or **Words**, find the word, then choose the analysis and the opinion you want for it: approve or disapprove it, or make it Unknown. Opinions change one analysis at a time, in the text. To keep one reading at several places of the same word, use the word panel described in [Passage](guide:passage). The available action may vary with the word’s current state and the reading you select.

Each word has two buttons. The first is its opinion mark: **A**, **U**, **D**, or a dashed mark when FieldWorks holds no analysis. Choose **Set analysis** to see each stored analysis and choose **Set analysis: Approved**, **Set analysis: Unknown**, **Set analysis: Disapproved** or **Set analysis: Remove**, or to mark the spelling Incorrect. The current Opinion is shown without staging it again. Once you stage a change, the mark turns solid. The second button is a number: how many readings PanGloss found that FieldWorks does not hold. Choose it to open the word panel for that word at that place, where you choose one reading and approve it for the places you check. Ctrl+ZCtrl+Z (⌘+Z on macOS) undoes the last staged choice.

The change is kept as pending work for this project. It applies to the word form everywhere, not only the occurrence you were looking at. Open **Proposals** and look under **Your Changes Not Applied Yet** to inspect it. Nothing is written to FieldWorks while you are choosing or reviewing.

To measure the effect before applying, open that document and choose **Check These Changes**. When you are ready, close FieldWorks and choose **Apply…**, then confirm. See [Apply to FieldWorks](guide:apply-to-fieldworks) for the conditions that must be met first.

## Inside a Proposal

When a Proposal is open, a word card adds a block called **In PanGloss · with this Proposal**. It shows the analyses PanGloss built for the word when the Proposal was last tried, and for each one the changes in the Proposal that built it. If the Proposal has not been tried yet the block says **Not tried yet**, while it is being tried it says **Trying…**, and if the project or the Proposal changed since, it says **Needs another try**. Nothing is tried again on its own.

Choose **Set analysis** to stage a change into the open Proposal instead of your pending word changes. **Approve … in** the Proposal's name approves an analysis FieldWorks already holds as Unknown that the Proposal now builds. **Add an expected parse to** the Proposal's name adds an analysis FieldWorks does not hold, as Approved, and the Proposal shows it as **Will add as Approved**. Either way the change is checked against the Proposal's own copy of the project, and it is applied together with the Proposal's other changes. If that copy has been cleaned up, the change is marked as needing another check; choose **Try again** on the Proposal bar.

Outside a Proposal nothing changes: your choices go to the pending word changes as before.

![A pending choice shown on its word card](shot:explained-word-card/unknown-staged)

entries.title: Compare Proposals
entries.description: Check two Proposals in Proposals, then choose Compare 2 Proposals. The comparison shows exactly that pair side by side. Choose Back to Proposals to return to the open documents; your edits and checks are still there.
entries.helpPage:
# Compare Proposals

Check two Proposals in **Proposals**, then choose **Compare 2 Proposals**. The comparison shows exactly that pair side by side. Choose **Back to Proposals** to return to the open documents; your edits and checks are still there.

Each side shows the Proposal's name, status, Rationale, the changes it makes to the grammar and its Comments count. **Will Fill In** and **Will Change** list the words each Proposal affects. **Where They Differ** lists the words whose effect differs between the two, with **Show in Texts** for each.

Motif compares two Proposals only when it can show they were measured the same way: the same project, baseline grammar, Text, decisions, parser and tokenizer, with a complete search for every listed word. When any of that is missing or has changed, the comparison says **Outdated** or **Comparison Unavailable**, gives the reason and offers **Measure Both Again**. Motif never subtracts two measurements it cannot match, and an unmeasured or incomplete word is never shown as no change.

Two Proposals that change some of the same words overlap. Overlap alone does not show which is better. Evidence covers a single Text, and the exact approved places a Proposal stops filling in are not available, so the comparison does not list them.

Applying one Proposal marks the other out of date until its evidence is refreshed. Each side has its own **Apply…** and follows the usual confirmation. See [Proposals](guide:proposals), [Review a Proposal](guide:review-a-proposal) and [Apply to FieldWorks](guide:apply-to-fieldworks).

entries.title: Default Selection
entries.description: The Default Selection is the set of Texts and added words Motif measures when you run the project without choosing another Selection. Motif saves it with the project. Each parse keeps the exact word list it measured, so changing the Default Selection does not rewrite earlier results.
entries.helpPage:
# Default Selection

The [Default Selection](term:default-selection) is the set of Texts and added words Motif measures when you run the project without choosing another Selection. Motif saves it with the project. Each [parse](term:parse-all-words) keeps the exact word list it measured, so changing the Default Selection does not rewrite earlier results.

The first time you set up a project, choose texts and add any extra words in **What Should Motif Measure Every Time?** Choose **Configure…** from the project menu to edit that choice later. The Selection needs at least one text or added word before Motif can parse. Setup, Settings, and **Analysis Options** in Texts → Sources edit the same saved parsing policy; see [Settings](guide:settings) for its time-limit choices.

The Default Selection is not a search query that changes behind your back. Motif resolves the chosen material for each run and records what it measured. After saving in FieldWorks, press **Refresh** to read the saved project, then choose **Parse all words** to measure the current Default Selection again.

The FieldWorks Text choices in **Texts → Sources** edit the current Selection. External Source **Context** changes instead stage a Proposal; **Current Chapter** stays local. See [Sources](guide:sources).

entries.title: Diagnostics
entries.description: Turn on Diagnostics in the health details or the View menu to add this page to the rail. Inspect the stored grammar check and recorded parser work here. The choice belongs to you and starts off. Turning Diagnostics off closes Diagnostics and removes diagnostic details from the window.
entries.helpPage:
# Diagnostics

Turn on Diagnostics in the health details or the View menu to add this page to the rail. Inspect the stored grammar check and recorded parser work here. The choice belongs to you and starts off. Turning Diagnostics off closes Diagnostics and removes diagnostic details from the window.

Diagnostics has exactly two tabs: **Warnings** and **Speed by Rule**. Opening the page does not start a parse or a grammar check. Opening either tab reads stored evidence and never starts Parsimony. Missing or outdated evidence is unavailable, rather than a count of zero.

In **Warnings**, select a recorded kind to read its explanation, named FieldWorks objects and attributed words. **Show Words** brings the selected warning's recorded word evidence into view. Exact uses, possible membership matches and spelling matches remain distinct. **Hide This Warning** hides a finding for you only; unhide it under **Settings → Hidden Warnings**. The warning count shows how many are hidden, and hiding never changes the grammar.

**Speed by Rule** shows recorded parser steps per measured word. Its denominator says how many selected words recorded work. The unattributed remainder stays visible. A missing denominator leaves the count unavailable. Partial per-word detail is labelled even when complete stored aggregate totals can be shown. Select a rule to resolve its exact **Open in FieldWorks** destination; unresolved objects have no link.

Rules are read and edited in FieldWorks. Warnings and Parsimony are advice and add no condition to Apply. A Proposal's Diagnostics uses only evidence bound to that Proposal's content and Trial. Missing, inconclusive or outdated Parsimony is never described as no change. Signed grammar-size changes remain unavailable when the stored contract does not supply them.

entries.title: Stale numbers and changes
entries.description: In the window, Motif marks a pending change as No longer fits when the FieldWorks project has changed something that choice depended on, such as the word form or an analysis. This means the pending choice cannot safely be applied as written. It is different from stale numbers, which mean stored measurement evidence describes an earlier project state.
entries.helpPage:
# Stale numbers and changes

In the window, Motif marks a pending change as [**No longer fits**](term:drift) when the FieldWorks project has changed something that choice depended on, such as the word form or an analysis. This means the pending choice cannot safely be applied as written. It is different from stale numbers, which mean stored measurement evidence describes an earlier project state.

For steps to check or remove a change, see **When a change no longer fits**.

entries.title: Archiphonemes and the glottal stop
entries.description: An archiphoneme is a sound that an underlying form carries and a rule changes. The nasal of a prefix such as paN- is one example: it is m, n or ng by the sound after it, and never N. LibLCM has no archiphoneme flag, and neither HermitCrab nor PanGloss treats one specially. It is a plain phoneme, so Motif authors it with Author a phoneme like any other.
entries.helpPage:
# Archiphonemes and the glottal stop

An archiphoneme is a sound that an underlying form carries and a rule changes. The nasal of a prefix such as `paN-` is one example: it is `m`, `n` or `ng` by the sound after it, and never `N`. LibLCM has no archiphoneme flag, and neither HermitCrab nor PanGloss treats one specially. It is a plain phoneme, so Motif authors it with [Author a phoneme](cmd:compose-author-phoneme) like any other.

## Encode the pattern

1. Choose a letter or symbol that the written language never uses for another sound, and author it as a phoneme (`compose-author-phoneme`). If the symbol is not a letter of the writing system, make it a word-forming character of the vernacular writing system first, or the form that holds it cannot be split into phonemes.
2. Give the phonemes of the surface sounds their features: define the features with `compose-author-phonological-feature`, then set them with `compose-edit-phoneme-features`. A natural class by features (`compose-author-natural-class`, `compose-edit-natural-class-features`) then picks out the conditioning sounds.
3. Write the underlying form of the affix or stem with the archiphoneme (`compose-author-lexical-entry`, `compose-author-alternate-form`), and add the rule that changes it (`compose-author-phonological-rule`).
4. Run a Trial with a word for each surface sound and with words that must not parse.

A rule that only changes the archiphoneme near some sounds leaves it in place elsewhere. If it must always change, add a rule for the elsewhere case.

## What Motif checks

Motif reports, with code `grammar.phoneme-never-used` at level information, a phoneme that no form, wordform, rule, natural class or environment uses. An archiphoneme without an underlying form, or one whose rule was never written, is reported until it is used. An inventory authored ahead of the lexicon is also reported; nothing needs changing then.

## The glottal stop

The glottal stop is an ordinary phoneme too. Two choices decide how it shows in a word:

- The orthography writes it, with a hyphen or an apostrophe or a letter. Author the phoneme with that representation. A hyphen or an apostrophe is a word-forming character only if the writing system says so.
- The orthography leaves it out where it is predictable, for example at the end of a word. Author the phoneme with a symbol that never appears in text, and let a rule delete or realise it, as for an archiphoneme.

Decide from the attested spellings, and ask the linguist when they do not decide it (guide ask-the-linguist).

## Pitfalls

- Do not author a second phoneme for a surface variant that a rule can derive.
- Do not remove an unused archiphoneme while a rule that will use it is still planned.
- Segment classes in a rewrite rule behave the same in a featureless project and in one with features (guide nasal-assimilation).

entries.title: Ask the linguist when evidence runs out
entries.description: Ask when two analyses fit the evidence and choosing between them changes the Proposal. A useful question lets the linguist distinguish those analyses using forms already in the project and one concrete prediction.
entries.helpPage:
# Ask the linguist when evidence runs out

Ask when two analyses fit the evidence and choosing between them changes the Proposal. A useful question lets the linguist distinguish those analyses using forms already in the project and one concrete prediction.

## Guess, ask or defer

- **Guess** only a low-impact, reversible choice that the existing evidence supports; keep it in a Draft and check it with a Dry Run and Trial.
- **Ask** when the linguist can answer a concrete contrast. Ask one question at a time and show the evidence plus the competing predictions.
- **Defer** when the project lacks the forms or the linguist cannot yet distinguish the choices. State what evidence would resolve the choice, and do not invent a Proposal.
- **Say the tool is missing** when Motif cannot create a required FieldWorks object. Explain the needed encoding and wait for a composer; do not imitate it with a different object.

When the project has no evidence for requested forms, do not suggest an affix shape, allomorph or example word, even as a prediction or an unapplied draft. Say what attested forms and contexts would resolve the question, then ask for them.

For example: “I can’t determine this pattern from the project. Could you share attested forms in the relevant contexts, including a contrasting form if available?”

## Build the question from evidence

Read forms with `motif_lexicon`, `motif_word` or `motif_texts`. Use the actual spellings and contexts returned for this project. Do not present guessed forms as attested; when requested forms are absent, ask for attested forms instead of predicting spellings.

Use this frame and replace every bracketed item with project evidence:

> “I found `<attested form A>` in `<observed context A>` and `<attested form B>` in `<observed context B>`. The two analyses predict `<predicted form A>` versus `<predicted form B>` for `<unobserved or contrasting context>`. Which form would a speaker use there?”

Ask for the missing fact only. Do not bundle a request to choose the analysis, name a rule, provide more examples and approve a Proposal into one question.

## Common wrong choices

- Guessing a high-impact choice the evidence does not support.
- Asking several questions at once, or with forms that are not attested in the project.

entries.title: Phonologically conditioned allomorphs
entries.description: A linguist sees one morpheme with different spoken or written forms in different sound contexts. FieldWorks can keep those forms together and condition each one on its surrounding sounds.
entries.helpPage:
# Phonologically conditioned allomorphs

A linguist sees one morpheme with different spoken or written forms in different sound contexts. FieldWorks can keep those forms together and condition each one on its surrounding sounds.

## Encode the pattern

- Keep the variants under one lexical entry when the evidence supports one morpheme.
- Give each variant the sound environment where it occurs. Use a natural class when several sounds share the relevant property.
- Put the narrowest conditioned forms before a less restricted or elsewhere form.
- Do not duplicate the same unrestricted form for every stem. Do not use an environment broader than the evidence, such as “after any consonant” when only one class is supported.
- Check whether the forms are truly one morpheme before treating their difference as phonological conditioning.

Existing ordinary alternate text can be edited in place with [Edit an allomorph form](cmd:compose-edit-allomorph-form) (`motif_edit_allomorph_form`), naming its expected owner, writing system and current text. This keeps conditions and references on the same form ID. Lexeme forms use [Rewrite lexeme forms](cmd:compose-rewrite-lexeme-form) with explicit `newForm` and `foldStressMarks=false` when underlying distinctions condition the grammar. [Edit a citation form](cmd:compose-edit-citation-form) (`motif_edit_citation_form`) retains a selected marked source headword separately from parser forms.

## Motif support

`motif_lexicon` with detailed results can read existing allomorphs and their environments. `motif_grammar` can read natural classes and environments. `motif_add_phoneme`, `motif_add_natural_class` and `motif_add_environment` create the sound inventory and context. `motif_add_lexeme_form` changes an existing lexeme form. `motif_add_alternate_form` creates a stem or affix alternate under an existing entry. It accepts optional sound `environments` and, for affix forms, optional `inflectionClasses`. When alternates already exist, supply an exact `placement` gap. `motif_add_affix_process_allomorph` adds a pattern-based form (an affix process with its own input and output) to an affix entry whose other forms may be plain allomorphs or processes; it takes no environments and applies to all of the entry's grammatical info. `motif_add_alternate_form` likewise adds a plain affix allomorph beside process forms. Both take `inflectionClasses` for inflectional grammatical info; the parser ignores them for a derivational analysis (the stem features an allomorph requires, `MsEnvFeatures` in LibLCM, are read for a derivational affix too, but Motif has no composer for them yet), so a mixed entry can use them for its inflectional analysis while restricting the derivational analysis through the `motif_edit_derivational_affix_restriction` MCP tool or `compose-edit-derivational-affix-restriction` CLI verb (guide suffix-prefix-slots). When the entry has no inflectional grammatical info, Motif refuses `inflectionClasses` and points to that composer. `motif_edit_allomorph_condition`, when selected by the profile, can link an environment to an existing allomorph.

## What an allomorph can and cannot carry

FieldWorks holds the meaning of a morpheme on the entry, not on its forms. So one form cannot have its own tense, gloss or slot.

| An allomorph can carry | An allomorph cannot carry |
|---|---|
| Sound environments the form occurs in (`environments`) | Its own gloss, tense or other label |
| Inflection classes of the stems it attaches to, for an inflectional analysis (`inflectionClasses`) | Its own grammatical info or slot |
| For an affix, the stem features and category it needs (conditions on the stem it attaches to) | A different category or meaning from the entry's other forms |
| For a stem, a stem name tied to inflection features | A rule to apply or skip (use exception features on the analysis) |
| Its place in the order of the entry's forms | Anything that changes which senses it serves |
| Being abstract (a form no word shows) | |

When the form needs a different label, as a past form beside a future one, make it its own entry with its own grammatical info, slot and sense. Two analyses on one entry do not help: the parser gives every form of the entry to every analysis, so both labels would apply to both forms.

## Two forms that must not block each other (free variation)

An earlier form with an environment blocks every later form of the same entry wherever it matches, the lexeme form (always last) included. HermitCrab's one exception is free fluctuation: neighbouring forms whose environment sets are exactly equal are not disjunctive, so both parse and neither blocks the other. For an affix this is the only encoding; an affix variant entry is not read by the parser. A stem can also be a variant entry with no sense of its own, which the parser loads as a separate stem, but that is a different morpheme, not a form of this one.

- To let the plain suffix `an` and a variant that starts with a hyphen character, `-an`, both parse after any sound, give the entry two forms with no environment. `motif_add_alternate_form` with no `environments` does this; leave the new form last, beside the unrestricted lexeme form. A real-parser test (`AuthorFreeVariationParserTests`) shows two spellings (`an` and `ang`) both parse after `o` and after `a`.
- Two alternates that carry the same environments are free variation with each other (the same test file shows both parse where the environment matches, and the plain lexeme form is blocked there). A form whose environments differ from its neighbour's is not free variation. An alternate restricted to "after a consonant" blocks the lexeme form after every consonant, so the plain spelling stops parsing there. The parser has no way to say "this form where the environment matches, and the plain form everywhere as well".
- Best workaround when the variant should occur only in one context but the plain form must stay possible there too: make the variant unrestricted (free variation) and accept that it also licenses the variant in other contexts, such as a hyphen after a vowel; measure that over-generation with a Trial.

## A hyphenated spelling of an affix process

An affix process cannot carry a written alternate form: it has no spelling of its own, only an input and an output. When the text writes a hyphen between the affix and the stem (Cebuano `l`-forms and `X-X` reduplication), make the hyphen part of the output. Add a second process to the same entry with `compose-author-affix-process-allomorph` (`motif_add_affix_process_allomorph`) whose output inserts the hyphen phoneme where the text writes it, for example `{"insert":["<i>","<k>","<a>","<hyphen>"]},{"copy":"rest"}` beside the process that inserts the same sounds without the hyphen. The hyphen must be a phoneme (`compose-author-phoneme`). LibLCM holds the entry's processes as ordered alternate forms of one entry, so both spellings share its gloss and grammatical info and the real parser reads either; for full reduplication a single process that copies the stem, inserts the hyphen and copies it again already gives the hyphenated spelling, so no second process is needed. A plain written alternate (`compose-author-alternate-form`) may share the entry with processes when it expresses a written realization rather than a pattern change.

Do not add a shape-restricted solid form to the entry of an unrestricted hyphen form. A form earlier in the order blocks every later form of the entry for the stems it matches, so a solid form restricted to, say, three-sound stems stops the hyphen spelling of exactly those stems (`RealParserReduplicationBlockingTests` shows `pul-pul` lost while `kaun-kaun` still parses). That is the loss an earlier round saw when it put shape forms on the hyphen entry. Give the restricted solid form its own entry: both spellings then parse, each by its own entry.

## Replace a process with a plain archiphoneme form

Keep the entry, its senses and grammatical analyses. In one Draft, author a plain alternate with `compose-author-alternate-form`, then move each prohibition occurrence to that form with [Retarget a prohibition](cmd:compose-edit-adhoc-prohibition-references). Use [Delete a prohibition](cmd:compose-delete-adhoc-prohibition) for restrictions that should disappear. Supply the complete expected state, including Disabled and legacy allomorph references. Morpheme prohibitions can keep their grammatical-analysis references when the entry and analyses stay the same.

Finally use [Delete an affix process](cmd:compose-delete-affix-process) with `entry`, the process `form` and the plain form as `replacement`. A lexeme process is replaced by promoting the plain alternate; an alternate process is removed while the plain form stays. The command refuses until every reference into the process graph has moved or gone, naming each remaining occurrence and its remedy. These steps can be one `compose` request, with an earlier step's created form referenced by its label. MCP stages only; a person reviews the Dry Run and Trial and Applies.

An archiphoneme is an ordinary phoneme whose spelling the plain form carries. Author its sound rule separately. Trial the unaffected forms and the forms the prohibitions exclude, as well as forms changed by the rule; a structural replacement alone does not prove parse preservation.

## One form blocked after one form of another affix

Sometimes one form of an affix is wrong only after one particular form of an earlier affix: a stative `-lik` fits after an applicative `-o` but not after `-e`, while `-k` fits after both. Create an allomorph prohibition with the CLI verb `compose-author-adhoc-prohibition`, which MCP offers as `motif_author_adhoc_prohibition` (kind `allomorph`; the later form as `first`, the earlier form as `rest`, adjacency `adjacent-to-right`). The parser drops only that pair of forms. Use it between forms of different entries: in an inflectional template an entry fills one slot, so a rule between two forms of the same entry would never fire there. To choose between forms of one entry, give each its own environment, or put the narrowest first and the general form last.

## Every sound except some, and a zero form chosen by class

A natural class is a fixed list of sounds (or of feature values), and FieldWorks has no complement or negated class. A project file can hold a negated feature value (LibLCM stores one), but FieldWorks' parser loader cannot read it and FieldWorks offers no way to make one, so do not rely on it; the grammar check warns (`grammar.negated-feature-value`) when a project holds one. For "every consonant except `<sound>`", list the sounds wanted (author the class with `motif_add_natural_class`) and add a sound to it when the inventory grows. A zero affix that should depend on the stem's class, not on the sounds around it, takes `inflectionClasses` (`motif_add_lexical_entry`, or `motif_add_alternate_form` for a form of an existing entry) and no environment; a stem of any other class gets no reading from it.

## Circumfix parts

Each part of a circumfix keeps its own environment on the real parser (a real-parser test, `RealParserCircumfixEnvironmentTests`, authors `ma-` with `-ang` after a consonant and `-x` after a vowel as two circumfix entries, each part with its own environment, and the parser chooses by the stem's last sound; the prefix part's environment is tested at the stem start and the suffix part's at the stem end). A part whose environment names the other part's side can never hold, so give each part a context on its own side of the stem. Run a Trial with the words each way: a missing half, the wrong linker and a stem the prefix environment excludes all stay unparsed.

## Check with a Trial

After a composer can express the change, include attested words from each sound context and words just outside those contexts. Confirm each variant appears where expected and that the unrestricted form does not win before a narrower variant. Include words that should remain unchanged.

## Ask the linguist

Ask when the evidence does not show whether the variants share a morpheme or what sound defines the environment. Use real project forms: “I found `<attested form A>` before `<observed sound class A>` and `<attested form B>` before `<observed sound class B>`. Does `<variant>` also occur before `<attested sound C>`, or is that a separate morpheme?” Replace bracketed items with forms read from this project; label any unobserved form as a prediction.

## Common wrong choices

- A separate entry for each variant of one morpheme.
- An environment broader than the evidence, or an unrestricted form placed before narrower ones.
- Listing variants for a regular sound change across many forms; a phonological rule fits that better.
- A new entry for each pattern-based form of one affix, or a plain alternate form for a pattern change; use `motif_add_affix_process_allomorph`.

entries.title: Feature-conditioned template slots
entries.description: A linguist sees an affix change with a grammatical value such as person, number or noun class. FieldWorks records those values on grammatical analyses and uses them to restrict which affix can fill a template slot.
entries.helpPage:
# Feature-conditioned template slots

A linguist sees an affix change with a grammatical value such as person, number or noun class. FieldWorks records those values on grammatical analyses and uses them to restrict which affix can fill a template slot.

## Encode the pattern

- Declare a feature and its values when the distinction has grammatical meaning the rest of the analysis needs to see.
- Put a noun's gender pair (for example 7/8) on the stem's grammatical analysis and its number on the class prefix's required features: each reading shows the prefix's number, the stem's gender filters which prefixes fit, and a number requirement never filters a stem that lacks one.
- Make two affixes in different slots agree (a subject marker and a relative marker, say) by giving both the same feature value in their required features: the parser keeps each affix's requirement on the word, so a pair that disagrees has no analysis. Use one feature whose values are the agreement groups, and give an affix that serves two groups one entry per group. Do not use this where the second affix agrees with something else, such as a suffix relative that agrees with the object.
- Put the supported value on the stem's grammatical analysis. Restrict an inflectional affix to its required feature values, then link it to the appropriate slot.
- Keep the template for the shared order of positions. Use separate templates only when forms have different required positions; use an optional slot only when that position may truly be absent.
- A template cannot be limited to a stem inflection class: FieldWorks ties a template to a category and the parser reads no class on it. To give one class its own affixes, restrict each affix in that template's slots to the class (`inflectionClasses` on `motif_add_lexical_entry` or `motif_add_alternate_form`, or `compose-edit-affix-inflection-classes`) or require a feature value on the affix. A stem of another class then finds no complete template; an optional slot lets it pass without the affix.
- Do not use an arbitrary inflection class for a value that must participate in agreement. Do not let every affix compete in the slot without the feature restrictions the data supports.

## Motif support

`motif_grammar` can read features, feature values, inflection classes and templates. `motif_add_inflection_feature` declares a closed morphosyntactic feature with its named values, and `motif_add_inflection_class` creates a category-owned class that can be assigned to a stem MSA through `motif_add_lexical_entry`. `motif_add_affix_slot` and `motif_add_affix_template` create the category-owned positions and their order. `motif_add_feature_structure` creates an empty feature structure on an existing or earlier-staged stem, inflectional affix or derivational affix MSA (a derivational affix takes side from or to), refusing an occupied slot. Use its returned exact structure identity with `motif_add_feature_value` to require a closed-feature specification, optionally selecting an existing value belonging to that exact feature. Inflectional affix selections are requirements on the word, not output features; their definitions must belong to the current morphosyntactic feature system and any declared structure type. A stem's values remain separate from the affix's requirements. `motif_remove_feature_value` removes one feature's specification from a stem or affix structure, including a derivational affix's From or To structure.

## Check with a Trial

Try words with each attested value and a contrasting value. Confirm the right affix appears for each value, the wrong affix does not, and a word with missing or incompatible information does not acquire an unsupported analysis. Include negative words and any known exceptions.

## Ask the linguist

Ask when it is unclear whether a contrast is grammatical agreement or arbitrary lexical grouping, or which value belongs to a form. Use attested forms: “`<attested form A>` takes `<affix A>` and is marked `<observed value A>`; `<attested form B>` takes `<affix B>`. Does `<attested form C>` have value `<value A>` or `<value B>`?” Replace bracketed items with project evidence and ask only the question that distinguishes the encodings.

## Common wrong choices

- An arbitrary inflection class for a value that must agree with other words.
- Letting every affix compete for a slot without feature restrictions the data supports.
- A separate affix or slot per feature value.

entries.title: Feature changes and alpha variables
entries.description: A feature change sets named features on the segment matched by the Input and preserves its other features. Use it for a regular alternation such as voicing, nasalisation or place assimilation. Follow Andy Black's section 6.3.2: an archiphoneme N takes its place from the following consonant across a morpheme boundary, N → [α place] /  + [α place].
entries.helpPage:
# Feature changes and alpha variables

A feature change sets named features on the segment matched by the Input and preserves its other features. Use it for a regular alternation such as voicing, nasalisation or place assimilation. Follow Andy Black's section 6.3.2: an archiphoneme N takes its place from the following consonant across a morpheme boundary, `N → [α place] / _ + [α place]`.

First define the phonological features and their values with [Author a phonological feature](cmd:compose-author-phonological-feature), give the phonemes their features with [Edit a phoneme's features](cmd:compose-edit-phoneme-features), and create the feature natural classes with [Author a natural class](cmd:compose-author-natural-class). Each surface phoneme needs enough features to distinguish it from the others (Black section 6.2). An underlying archiphoneme may leave place unspecified. A separate feature can distinguish underlying N from surface nasals; the Output then sets that feature to its surface value as well as copying place.

## Feature change

An Output item uses `change`, an array of `{ "feature": "<feature-id>", "value": "<value-id>" }` pairs. These are feature and value identities from this project's phonological feature system. A plus or minus feature value is an ordinary value identity, distinct from the polarity of an alpha reference. For example:

```json
{
  "name": "voice the matched consonant",
  "direction": "simultaneous",
  "input": [{ "naturalClass": "<voiceless-consonant-class-id>" }],
  "output": [{ "change": [{ "feature": "<voice-id>", "value": "<plus-id>" }] }]
}
```

The Output changes voice and keeps place and manner. Motif creates a feature natural class (`PhNCFeatures`) for this partial description, as FieldWorks does. Input and Output must have the same number of items when an Output item uses `change`, so each change has a matched segment. A rule whose Output is a multi-member segment class does not choose a member. It applies only the features the members share, so the input segment keeps its own value for every feature the members differ on. An *l* stays *l* under {l,w}, and a [-lat] *d* becomes *r* under {r,l}. Only an input with no value for those features matches every member (fieldworks-parser-conformance#38). To change named features, use a feature natural class at an aligned Output position; for free variation, use alternate forms of the stem.

## Alpha agreement and disagreement

A `variables` array adds alpha references to a feature natural class in Input or either context, or to an Output `change`. Each reference contains a `variable` name, a closed phonological `feature` identity, and `polarity` (`+` by default). Use the same variable name for the same feature everywhere in that rule. Plus requires agreement with the variable; minus requires disagreement. Either polarity can bind a variable, and a variable may have a single reference. A minus is not a fixed minus feature value. FieldWorks' loader can name at most 24 distinct alpha variables across the whole rule, including all right-hand sides; Motif refuses a larger rule before staging it.

Here is the Black section 6.3.2 shape. The archiphoneme class matches N, the following-consonant class supplies place, and the Output makes a surface nasal with that place:

```json
{
  "name": "nasal place assimilation",
  "direction": "simultaneous",
  "input": [{ "naturalClass": "<archiphoneme-class-id>" }],
  "output": [{
    "change": [{ "feature": "<archiphoneme-feature-id>", "value": "<surface-value-id>" }],
    "variables": [{ "variable": "alpha", "feature": "<place-id>", "polarity": "+" }]
  }],
  "right": [
    { "boundary": "morpheme" },
    { "naturalClass": "<following-consonant-class-id>",
      "variables": [{ "variable": "alpha", "feature": "<place-id>", "polarity": "+" }] }
  ]
}
```

With underlying N + pa, N + ta and N + ka, expect mpa, nta and ŋka; npa, mta and the other wrong nasals have no analysis. Check each place and negative controls with a Trial before Apply. For a binary feature, Output polarity `-` and context polarity `+` express dissimilation instead. An empty `change` is allowed when alpha supplies the change by itself.

Motif refuses one variable naming different features, duplicate or contradictory polarities on one item, and a fixed and variable value for the same feature on one item. A referenced feature must be a declared closed feature with values in this project; it need not occur on any phoneme. Alpha references belong to feature natural classes, not literal phoneme or boundary items. They are not available in allomorph environment strings. FieldWorks' current loader cannot discover a variable used only inside optional or repeated items in multi-item contexts, so Motif explains this limit before staging such a rule. The same variable is discoverable when it also occurs on Input, Output, an ordinary context item, or a context containing only the repeated item.

## Read and edit

[Author a sound rule](cmd:compose-author-phonological-rule) and [Edit a sound rule](cmd:compose-edit-phonological-rule) accept these items through `--intent`. Their MCP tools stage the same intent in a Draft; a person Applies the Proposal.

Read `motif_grammar(kind="phonological_rules", detail="detailed")` before editing. Copy its `intent` into `expected`, and use its returned variable identifiers in changed parts to keep sharing with parts left in place. Read-back uses each stored feature constraint's identity as the variable name; author-supplied labels are local to authoring and are not stored by LibLCM. If every reference is in replaced Input, the constraint is recreated with a new identity while its sharing and polarity stay the same. Feature Output classes read back with their `naturalClass` identities and alpha references, preserving sharing with other users of the class. Multiple right-hand sides read back as an ordered `rightHandSides` sequence with per-case Output, contexts, rule features and input categories. Replace that complete sequence under `expected.rightHandSides` to add, remove or reorder cases; alpha scope and sharing span the whole rule. Only an unrepresentable context or applicability reference prevents editable read-back.

The default PanGloss engine supports feature changes and alpha agreement. Its FST engine may refuse alpha rules. Alpha on Input is representable and supported by the FieldWorks loader, but hc.dll parsing parity for that shape is unproven because the oracle hangs. A segment unspecified for a feature does not satisfy a fixed minus value in a synthesis rule or its environment. A multi-member Output segment-list class does not supply alternatives, while multiple right-hand sides are ordered cases: the first applicable case wins. Rule features restrict each case but do not make overlapping cases optional. Metathesis is a separate capability.

entries.title: Segmental nasal assimilation
entries.description: A linguist sees a nasal change its sound near another consonant, while the morpheme remains the same. When the evidence supports a sound rule, FieldWorks can encode the change as a phonological rule instead of listing a separate affix spelling for every context.
entries.helpPage:
# Segmental nasal assimilation

A linguist sees a nasal change its sound near another consonant, while the morpheme remains the same. When the evidence supports a sound rule, FieldWorks can encode the change as a phonological rule instead of listing a separate affix spelling for every context.

## Encode the pattern

- First establish the underlying nasal and the contexts in which its surface form changes.
- Use phonological features or natural classes to describe the nasal, the conditioning sounds and the change. Keep the context narrow enough to exclude unrelated nasals and consonants.
- Use a regular segmental rule for a sound change across forms. Record rule order and whether the pattern applies simultaneously or iteratively when that affects the evidence.
- Do not duplicate a whole affix for each place of articulation when one rule accounts for the alternation. Do not write a rule that changes every nasal merely because some nasals assimilate.
- Treat deletion, exceptional spellings or lexical restrictions as separate decisions when the data supports them; do not hide them in an over-broad assimilation rule.

## Motif support

`motif_grammar` can read phonemes, natural classes and phonological rules. `motif_add_phoneme`, `motif_add_natural_class` and `motif_add_phonological_rule` create the sound inventory, reusable sound classes and regular rules. A rule intent names existing phonemes or natural classes in its input, output and contexts. `motif_edit_phonological_rule` changes a rule in place, `motif_order_phonological_rules` reorders rules, `motif_set_phonological_rule_disabled` turns one off or on, and `motif_delete_phonological_rule` removes one. A context item may be optional or repeated. Input and Output each accept up to eight phoneme or natural-class items in order, and may have different lengths. A segment-list natural class in the Output does not choose a member; it applies only the features its members share, and the input keeps its own value for the rest. An aligned feature-class Output changes the named features on the matched segment and preserves the rest; see [Feature rules](guide:encoding/feature-rules). Read `motif_grammar(kind="phonological_rules", detail="detailed")` to get the rule's `intent` for an edit's `expected` guard. `motif_add_phonological_feature` and `motif_add_phonological_feature_value` define the phonological features and their values, `motif_edit_phoneme_features` sets them on phonemes, and `motif_edit_natural_class_features` changes the feature constraints of a natural class; a class by features can be created with `motif_add_natural_class` (`features`). A nasal that changes with its neighbour is often an archiphoneme, a phoneme only the underlying form carries (`motif_guide(topic="archiphonemes")`). `motif_add_affix_process` and `motif_add_affix_process_allomorph` express a substitution as pattern-based forms of one affix instead. `motif_guide(topic="conditioned-allomorphs")` describes the related case where the evidence instead supports stored conditioned variants.

## Order the rules

Rules apply one after another, and a later rule sees the output of the earlier ones. A chain such as a place rule (a class becomes a nasal after the archiphoneme) followed by a deletion rule (the archiphoneme drops before a nasal) and an elsewhere rule (the archiphoneme becomes the velar nasal) works only in that order. If the elsewhere rule comes first, the archiphoneme is gone before the others see it and the words get no analysis. Reorder instead of rewriting; test a word for each branch. A segment-list natural class can also be used without phonological features. Feature-class rules require the relevant features and represented counterpart phonemes.

## Check with a Trial

Include attested forms for each conditioning place, forms where the nasal should stay unchanged, and negative words that should not become valid. Check that each output matches the evidence and that rule ordering does not alter unrelated segments.

## Ask the linguist

Ask when the forms do not decide whether the change is assimilation, a stored allomorph or a lexical exception. Build one contrast from actual project forms: “In `<attested form A>`, the nasal is before `<observed sound A>`; in `<attested form B>`, it is before `<observed sound B>`. Does the same morpheme occur before `<attested sound C>`, and what form do speakers use?” Replace bracketed items with evidence and distinguish observed forms from predictions.

## Common wrong choices

- Duplicating an affix for each place of articulation when one rule explains the alternation.
- An unconstrained affix process for a nasal change may require substantial parser work. Several processes kept as allomorphs of one Verb-only entry (the restriction comes from the entry's grammatical info; the composer has no category input), with `motif_add_affix_process_allomorph`, stopped no words with compounding off.
- A rule that changes every nasal because only some assimilate.

When only some prefixes substitute, the change is conditioned by the morpheme, not by sound alone. Cebuano is an example: Wolff treats substitution at the paN-, maN-, naN- and hiN- boundary as systematic (p, b become m; t, d, s become n; k and glottal stop become ng; l becomes ngl or nl, both accepted), while ning- and ming- keep k (ningkubit, mingkuyánap). Put the substituting forms on one entry as process allomorphs with `motif_add_affix_process_allomorph`, not in a phonological rule that would also apply to the prefixes that keep the consonant.

entries.title: A supported finding of no inflection
entries.description: A linguist may find that words keep the same form across grammatical contexts that another language marks with affixes. Motif should preserve that finding instead of inventing a prefix, suffix or template to match expectations from another language.
entries.helpPage:
# A supported finding of no inflection

A linguist may find that words keep the same form across grammatical contexts that another language marks with affixes. Motif should preserve that finding instead of inventing a prefix, suffix or template to match expectations from another language.

## Encode the pattern

- Compare the same lexemes across the grammatical contexts at issue. Check representative words and exceptions before deciding that there is no inflection.
- Leave out affix entries, slots and templates for a category when the evidence shows no inflectional form change there.
- Keep lexical meaning, part of speech and any grammatical features that the analysis actually needs. A language can have grammatical distinctions without marking them by affixes.
- Do not add a null affix or empty slot just to represent an assumed default. Do not conclude “no inflection” from one unchanged word or from missing data.

## Motif support

`motif_lexicon`, `motif_grammar` and `motif_word` can show the forms and analyses already recorded. `motif_add_lexeme_form` can edit an existing form, and `motif_add_feature_structure` can add an empty structure to an existing stem analysis; neither is needed to record the absence of an affix. No grammar composer is required to leave an unsupported affix out.

## Check with a Trial

Do not use a Trial as proof that an affix does not exist. If a Proposal changes nearby grammar, include representative unchanged forms and negative words in `motif_trial`; confirm they remain unchanged and do not gain analyses from the new rule. If there is no change to propose, report the evidence without creating an empty Proposal.

## Ask the linguist

Ask when the project lacks enough comparable forms to separate no inflection from missing or unrecorded data. Use attested examples: “`<attested form A>` and `<attested form B>` have the same form in the contexts recorded here. Are these the same lexeme in contrasting `<grammatical contexts>`, and is there another form speakers use?” Replace bracketed items with observed project data; do not state the absence as settled until the comparison is supported.

## Common wrong choices

- Inventing an affix or template because another language marks the distinction.
- Approximating a missing composer with unrelated edits.

entries.title: Authoring and editing phonological rules
entries.description: A regular rewrite rule shares its Input, name and direction across one or more right-hand sides. Each right-hand side has its own Output, left and right environments, required and excluded rule features, and optional input categories. Input and Output each contain up to eight ordered phoneme or natural-class items. Empty Input means insertion; empty Output means deletion. Context items can be optional or repeated and can name word and morpheme boundaries.
entries.helpPage:
# Authoring and editing phonological rules

A regular rewrite rule shares its Input, name and direction across one or more right-hand sides. Each right-hand side has its own Output, left and right environments, required and excluded rule features, and optional input categories. Input and Output each contain up to eight ordered phoneme or natural-class items. Empty Input means insertion; empty Output means deletion. Context items can be optional or repeated and can name word and morpheme boundaries.

## One rule, several outcomes

Wolff section 5.15 gives *kabukiran* and *kabukilan* from *bukid*. A rule cannot offer both. A rule whose Output is a multi-member segment class does not choose a member. It applies only the features the members share, so the input segment keeps its own value for every feature the members differ on. An *l* stays *l* under {l,w}, and a [-lat] *d* becomes *r* under {r,l}. Only an input with no value for those features matches every member (fieldworks-parser-conformance#38). Author a free d → r/l (or l → w) alternation as an alternate form of the stem on the existing entry, one per source-attested stem, so no second entry or analysis is needed. Use a rule only for a change that is obligatory where it applies: a literal phoneme or a feature-class Output, with a required exception feature on the stems the source selects. Tag only the analyses supported by the source: *sayran* does not license *saylan*. Preserve any quantity or environment conditions supported by the source and check both forms and untagged controls in a Trial.

Multiple right-hand sides are ordered cases, rather than freely alternating branches. FieldWorks uses the first applicable case at a matching site. Two overlapping d → r and d → l cases therefore do not produce both alternatives; an Output class supplies that choice within one case. Features restrict which words a case affects. They do not make overlapping cases optional or silently introduce dialect/register scope. Use explicit lexical features only where the evidence supports that distinction.

## Intent and guarded edits

[Author a sound rule](cmd:compose-author-phonological-rule) accepts `rightHandSides`, an array of one or more such cases, instead of the single-outcome `output`, `left` and `right` shorthand. The number of cases has no authoring ceiling. Within each case, `requiredFeatures` names the exception features or inflection classes the word must carry, and `excludedFeatures` names those it must carry none of. Omitting either means an empty set for that case. Features restrict applicability; they do not make overlapping cases optional or introduce a dialect or register model. A dialect distinction can be represented by explicit features on the appropriate analyses when the linguistic evidence supports it.

[Edit a sound rule](cmd:compose-edit-phonological-rule) replaces the complete `rightHandSides` sequence under `expected.rightHandSides`. Copy the detailed rule read into `expected`, then add, remove or reorder outcome objects. An unrestricted single-outcome read uses the older `output`, `left` and `right` form; copying all three into `expected` also guards its conversion to several outcomes. Omitted fields within a replacement outcome become empty, so retain its contexts and rule features when they should stay. Input, direction and rule name remain shared. [Feature changes and alpha variables](cmd:compose-author-phonological-rule) work within each case, with alpha identities shared across the whole rule.

Each outcome requires `output`. Its omitted `left`, `right`, `requiredFeatures`, `excludedFeatures` and `inputCategories` are empty lists. Rule features name exception features or inflection classes, and `inputCategories` names part-of-speech identities (including their subcategories). A feature cannot be both required and excluded in the same outcome. Different outcomes may have different sets. The single-outcome shorthand also accepts `inputCategories`, and [Set rule features](cmd:compose-edit-phonological-rule-features) edits it on an existing one-outcome rule; categories are required only, as FieldWorks stores no excluded category (Black 2025, section 6.1.2.2.1). Output `change` and `variables` use the feature-rules encoding contract; alpha identities are shared across the whole rule.

Read `motif_grammar(kind="phonological_rules", detail="detailed")` and retain the complete returned intent. A guarded sequence replacement creates fresh right-hand-side objects while keeping the rule's identity, position and disabled flag. Omitted fields inside replacement cases are cleared, so copy every restriction that should survive. A stale sequence, including a changed case order or applicability set, stages nothing. The older Output/context shorthand remains available for editing one outcome; on multiple outcomes use the complete sequence.

Example with distinct environments:

```json
{
  "name": "context-dependent nasal outcomes",
  "direction": "simultaneous",
  "input": [{ "phoneme": "<n-id>" }],
  "rightHandSides": [
    { "output": [{ "phoneme": "<m-id>" }], "right": [{ "phoneme": "<p-id>" }], "requiredFeatures": ["<tag-id>"] },
    { "output": [{ "phoneme": "<ng-id>" }], "right": [{ "phoneme": "<k-id>" }], "requiredFeatures": ["<tag-id>"] }
  ]
}
```

Before Apply, Dry Run and Trial words for every case, every lexical alternative and each negative control. Two sounds that trade places are a metathesis rule: use [Author a metathesis rule](cmd:compose-author-metathesis-rule).

entries.title: Prefix and suffix slots
entries.description: A linguist sees prefixes or suffixes recurring in the same grammatical order across words. FieldWorks represents each affix as a lexical entry and uses a template to say where it can occur.
entries.helpPage:
# Prefix and suffix slots

A linguist sees prefixes or suffixes recurring in the same grammatical order across words. FieldWorks represents each affix as a lexical entry and uses a template to say where it can occur.

## Encode the pattern

- Keep one affix entry for one morpheme, with its prefix or suffix morph type, form and grammatical analysis.
- Put inflectional affixes in slots owned by the part of speech they apply to. Put those slots in the template in the order speakers use them.
- Mark a slot optional only when that grammatical position may truly be absent. Use separate templates when forms have different required positions.
- Do not make a new affix entry for each stem that takes the same affix. Do not use one broad slot for affixes with different grammatical jobs.

## Motif support

`motif_grammar` can read categories, templates and slots. `motif_add_lexical_entry` creates one entry and one sense with a structured MSA: use an inflectional MSA for a slot-filling affix, or a derivational MSA with both its source and destination categories. `motif_add_affix_slot` creates a category-owned slot and can assign existing inflectional MSAs; `motif_add_affix_template` creates the ordered prefix and suffix slots. Use returned entity ids in later calls or batches after the creating call completes. Batch intents may reference only ids from earlier completed calls or batches; declare operation ordering and dependencies in the intent data, since array position alone does not establish them.

## Restricting which stems an affix attaches to

Where the restriction goes depends on the kind of affix, because FieldWorks' parser reads it from different places.

- Inflectional grammatical info: restrict the affix form to inflection classes. `motif_add_alternate_form` and `motif_add_affix_process_allomorph` take `inflectionClasses`, and `compose-edit-affix-inflection-classes` changes them later. FieldWorks reads the form's Inflection Classes for inflectional grammatical info only.
- Derivational grammatical info: use the `motif_edit_derivational_affix_restriction` MCP tool or `compose-edit-derivational-affix-restriction` CLI verb to set or clear its From Inflection Class and, optionally, set From Exception Features and To Exception Features (the features the derived stem receives); `alsoMsas` applies the same change to many affixes in one intent, and `compose-add-exception-features` adds features to many derivational affixes at once (`"side":"to"` for the To set). An affix process such as reduplication takes the same restriction, since the features sit on its grammatical info. FieldWorks reads those fields from the derivational grammatical info. Form inflection classes do not restrict a derivational analysis, so a mixed entry can use both paths for their corresponding analyses. If an entry has no inflectional grammatical info, Motif refuses form `inflectionClasses` and names the derivational restriction tool.
